page_summary:
The Jungle People is the canonical works-table record for PKD's short-story collection corpus item. The record links the archive's preserved manifestation of the work to the broader corpus and gives researchers a single place to follow its bibliographic and interpretive context.

The preserved archive item here is The Jungle People (Berkeley Daily Gazette, February 17, 1942) (1942).

The source record itself summarizes the work as follows: A 2-page scanned PDF of 'The Jungle People,' an early piece by Philip K. Dick published in the Berkeley Daily Gazette on February 17, 1942. No OCR text layer is present. Dick would have been approximately thirteen years old at the time of publication, making this among his earliest known published writings.

The Berkeley Daily Gazette was Dick's local newspaper during his childhood and adolescence in Berkeley, California. Publication at age thirteen demonstrates Dick's precocious literary ambition and the early development of his distinctive imaginative vision. The title 'The Jungle People' suggests an adventure or exotic fiction theme typical of juvenile writing. This document is of considerable biographical interest as evidence of Dick's earliest creative development and his initial entry into the world of published writing.

The entry is most useful when tracing publication context, later commentary, or relationships to other works.

summary: PKD (age 13) writes home from California Preparatory School in Ojai, defending his decision to stay despite homesickness and refusing his mother's offers to bring him home.
PKD's English-theme essay on a cat is read aloud to the class by Mr. Barnes after the first paragraph compels it — an early recognition of his prose.
